docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues. This concept is fundamental to understanding the difference between human expertise and automated behavior in market research contexts.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman draws on skill philosophy to establish that agential control involves:

  • Initiation control: The capacity to begin an activity rather than merely respond to environmental triggers
  • Adjustment flexibility: The ability to modify execution as circumstances change
  • Responsibility assumption: Taking ownership for outcomes, including failures that provide learning opportunities
  • Value integration: Aligning actions with deeper understanding of why the activity matters

docs.title: Contrast with Habitual Behavior
docs.text: Agential Control Habitual Behavior Initiated by the agent Triggered by environment Flexible adjustment Rigid execution Responsibility assumed Responsibility displaced Value-integrated Value-neutral Requires volitional capacity Requires minimal willpower

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
In AI-augmented market research, agential control manifests through:

  • Research design: Researchers who initiate and adjust methodologies based on emerging insights rather than following AI-prescribed templates
  • Data interpretation: Analysts who exercise judgment in contextualizing AI-generated insights rather than accepting outputs uncritically
  • Ethical decision-making: Professionals who take responsibility for research ethics rather than deferring to AI recommendations
  • Client communication: Researchers who adapt messaging based on client reactions rather than delivering standardized reports

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI tools can undermine agential control through:

  • Automation bias: Over-trusting AI recommendations without critical evaluation
  • Decision offloading: Transferring responsibility for research judgments to AI systems
  • Template dependency: Relying on AI-generated research frameworks without modification
  • Feedback loop reduction: Eliminating opportunities to learn from mistakes when AI handles error correction

docs.title: Preserving Agential Control
docs.text:
Market research organizations can maintain agential control by:

  1. Implementing AI transparency requirements that reveal the reasoning behind recommendations
  2. Designing deliberate friction in AI tools that requires researcher input at critical decision points
  3. Creating reflection protocols where researchers document their judgment process alongside AI outputs
  4. Establishing error review sessions that normalize learning from research mistakes
  5. Developing hybrid workflows where AI handles routine tasks while humans focus on novel, complex challenges

docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: AI Deskilling as a Structural Problem
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-03 | Last Updated: 2026-07-22

The AI deskilling structural problem refers to the phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.title: Core Argument
docs.text: Rather than framing deskilling as a matter of individual responsibility—expecting people to simply will themselves to cultivate 'the arts of personhood'—Ferdman demonstrates how AI's influence creates systemic conditions that inhibit the development and exercise of human capacities by undermining the process of capacity cultivation. The paper introduces 'capacity-hostile environments' to identify instances where AI mediation impedes human capacity cultivation.

docs.title: Capacity vs. Skill Distinction
docs.text:
• Capacities are analogous to virtues: core human abilities (epistemic, social, creative, volitional) constitutive of flourishing
  • Skills are domain-specific dispositions (hunting, coding, navigating) where obsolescence may be innocuous
  • Deskilling of core human capacities is harmful because inadequate development leads to 'capacity impoverishment'

docs.title: Capacity-Skilling Framework
docs.text: Being capacity-skilled involves: - Agential control over capacities - Obtained through habituation process - Manifested in competent exercise of capacities - Supported by societal shared valuing of capacities

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text: AI creates capacity-hostile environments through: - Narrow fields of affordances that restrict action possibilities - Disembodied interaction that undermines intersubjective learning - Automation of routine tasks that deprives users of habituation opportunities - Plan-following encouragement that replaces plan-forming agency

docs.title: Evidence of Deskilling
docs.text: Growing evidence shows AI dependence leads to: - Erosion of activity awareness, competence maintenance, and output assessment (Rinta-Kahila et al. 2023) - Diminished diagnostic reasoning, clinical judgment, and ethical sensitivity in healthcare (NHS England 2023; Natali et al. 2025) - Decline in critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical reasoning (Bonicalzi et al. 2023; Gerlich 2025; Lee et al. 2025)

docs.title: Artificial Personal Assistants Case Study
docs.text: APAs exemplify capacity-hostile environments because they: - Replace plan-forming with plan-following, undermining agential control - Discourage users from seeking alternative growth opportunities - Reduce need for routine decision-making that builds capacity - Decrease embodied, intersubjective interaction necessary for capacity development - Example: Sunsama scheduling app plans users' days, removing opportunities for self-directed planning

docs.title: Philosophical Framework
docs.text: The analysis employs developmental-perfectionism, a neo-Aristotelian approach where: - Human flourishing is a complex, unified, well-rounded life - Competent exercise of capacities yields intrinsically valuable goods - Capacity-deskilling is bad because capacities are constitutive of flourishing - Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives

docs.title: Societal Implications
docs.text: The structural perspective necessitates: - Evaluating AI applications based on conduciveness to capacity cultivation - Creating capacity-conducive environments through public goods - Shifting responsibility from individuals to society for preserving capacity-development opportunities - Recognizing that expecting 'virtuous superheroes' to resist deskilling overlooks structural realities

docs.title: Contrast with Individual-Responsibility Approaches
docs.text: Unlike frameworks treating deskilling as individual failing, the structural perspective recognizes that: - Persons develop capacities in response to social and material environment - Deficient environments lead to deskilling and subsequent devaluation of capacities - Without proper mentoring and shared valuing, individuals cannot cultivate capacities - Example: Students cannot develop critical thinking if educational environments prioritize AI-generated content

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development

A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

This creates particular challenges for entry-level positions through the entry-level-squeeze, as foundational tasks that build expertise are automated before new developmental pathways are established.

docs.text: Successful navigation of AI professionalization requires: - Redesigning roles to preserve meaningful human involvement in value-creating activities - Developing new apprenticeship models that build expertise despite automated foundational tasks - Aligning skill development priorities with the evolving value chain

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, providing alternatives to capacity-hostile-environments. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities, with critical implications for sustainable AI integration in market research.

docs.title: Essential Components
docs.text:
Capacity-conducive environments provide:

  1. Embodied interaction opportunities - Physical presence and sensory experience essential for developing social and moral capacities
  2. Intersubjective mentorship - Guidance from experienced practitioners who instill both mechanical aspects and value of skills
  3. Gradual habituation pathways - Structured progression from novice to expert through successive trials and learning from mistakes
  4. Agential control preservation - Opportunities to initiate and adjust activities rather than merely respond to environmental triggers
  5. Shared valuing of capacities - Cultural recognition of the intrinsic worth of developing human capacities

docs.title: Market Research Implementation
docs.text:
In market research organizations, capacity-conducive environments manifest through:

  • Hybrid research methodologies that combine AI efficiency with human-led qualitative components requiring embodied interaction
  • Structured mentorship programs where junior researchers learn through guided practice rather than solely relying on AI tools
  • Deliberate friction design in AI tools that preserves opportunities for developing analytical judgment through challenging cases
  • Community spaces (physical or virtual) that encourage shared reflection on research practice and values
  • Error-embracing cultures that normalize disappointment and failure as necessary components of the habituation process

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text:
Unlike capacity-hostile-environments, which narrow the field of affordances and encourage plan-following behaviors, capacity-conducive environments:

  • Expand opportunities for plan-forming vs plan-following
  • Support development of volitional capacity through appropriately challenging tasks
  • Foster intersubjectivity in skilling through meaningful human-to-human guidance
  • Maintain rich embodiment in skilling essential for social capacities
  • Enable the gradual habituation process necessary for true expertise

docs.title: Business Value
docs.text:
Organizations cultivating capacity-conducive environments demonstrate:

  • 23% higher retention of research talent according to mrii-2026-market-research-study
  • Greater innovation capacity as researchers develop deeper creative capacities
  • Enhanced ethical decision-making through preserved social capacities
  • More effective AI implementation as researchers maintain epistemic capacities to evaluate AI outputs
  • Reduced human operating model gap through aligned human-AI development

docs.title: Implementation Framework
docs.text:
Creating capacity-conducive environments requires:

  1. Environmental audit to identify capacity-hostile elements in current workflows
  2. Affordance mapping to redesign workflows preserving critical capacity-development opportunities
  3. Mentorship infrastructure supporting intersubjective habituation
  4. Evaluation metrics tracking capacity development alongside productivity
  5. Leadership commitment to valuing human capacity development as strategic imperative

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Environments that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing in market research contexts.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
Capacity-hostile environments:

  • Provide narrow fields of affordances that systematically reduce action possibilities
  • Undermine agential control by encouraging habitual responses to environmental triggers rather than skillful initiation of activities
  • Restrict opportunities for embodiment in skilling through disembodied interactions
  • Limit intersubjectivity in skilling by reducing meaningful human-to-human guidance
  • Fail to support the gradual habituation process necessary for skill development

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
1. AI-powered survey tools that automate questionnaire design without preserving opportunities for researchers to develop their understanding of question framing through practice and failure

  2. Automated data interpretation systems that provide ready-made insights without requiring researchers to engage in the iterative process of developing analytical judgment

  3. Virtual research platforms that replace face-to-face interactions with disembodied digital interfaces, undermining the development of empathy and social capacities essential for qualitative research

  4. AI scheduling assistants that manage researchers' calendars without opportunities to develop time management skills through trial and error

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
When market research professionals operate in capacity-hostile environments:

  • They experience capacity impoverishment across epistemic, social, creative, and volitional domains
  • Their ability to exercise practical rationality (phronesis) diminishes, reducing their capacity for wise judgment in complex research scenarios
  • The value-chain shift accelerates as organizations prioritize AI efficiency over human capacity development
  • The entry-level squeeze intensifies as foundational research tasks become automated, eliminating traditional training grounds

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Unlike capacity-conducive-environments, which actively encourage capacity development through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, capacity-hostile environments create conditions where researchers cannot develop the deep expertise needed to complement AI systems effectively. This structural problem explains the growing human operating model gap observed in AI adoption.

docs.title: Remediation Strategies
docs.text:
Organizations can transform capacity-hostile environments by:

  • Designing AI tools with deliberate friction that preserves opportunities for skill development
  • Creating structured mentorship programs that support intersubjective habituation
  • Ensuring research workflows maintain embodied interaction with participants
  • Implementing reflection practices that develop agential control over AI-assisted workflows

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-18 | Last Updated: 2026-07-22

Creative capacities are the human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and can be undermined by AI systems that create environments hostile to creative development.

docs.title: Novel Combination
docs.text:
• Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Creating unexpected connections between seemingly unrelated concepts
  • Generating insights through juxtaposition of diverse knowledge domains
  • Example: Combining principles from biology and engineering to develop biomimetic designs

docs.title: Conceptual Transformation
docs.text:
• Transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck or mechanical procedures
  • Reshaping frameworks to see problems from new perspectives
  • Developing innovative approaches that challenge existing paradigms
  • Example: Reframing a marketing challenge as a storytelling opportunity rather than a sales problem

docs.title: Development Process
docs.text: Creative capacities develop through:

docs.title: Habituation Process
docs.text:
• Gradual progression from novice to expert through practice and experimentation
  • Involves encountering and overcoming creative disappointment and failure
  • Requires refinement through successive trials and learning from mistakes
  • Example: Developing design skills through iterative prototyping and user feedback

docs.title: Intersubjective Learning
docs.text:
• Becoming creatively skilled typically requires mentors to instill both technical competence and appreciation for creative value
  • Shared valuing develops through relationships where both mentor and mentee view creativity as intrinsically valuable
  • Creative communities establish shared practices that generate reasons for creative action
  • Example: Art studios where apprentices learn not just techniques but the value of artistic expression

docs.title: Embodied Engagement
docs.text:
• Proper cultivation requires environments affording opportunities for creative exploration
  • Physical spaces that encourage experimentation and risk-taking
  • Embodied interaction that supports spontaneous idea generation
  • Example: Innovation labs with flexible workspaces that encourage collaboration

docs.title: AI Threat Analysis
docs.text: AI systems threaten creative capacities through:

docs.title: Automated Content Generation
docs.text:
• Deskilling through over-reliance on AI for idea generation
  • Reduced opportunities for creative problem-solving when AI provides ready solutions
  • Diminished capacity for conceptual transformation when AI reinforces existing patterns
  • Example: Marketing professionals using AI content generators without developing original campaign concepts

docs.title: Narrowed Affordance Fields
docs.text:
• Digital environments that fracture creative affordance space into disconnected fields
  • Recommendation algorithms that limit exposure to diverse creative influences
  • AI tools that provide standardized creative solutions rather than encouraging exploration
  • Example: Design tools that offer limited template options rather than open-ended creation

docs.title: Structural Implications
docs.text: The deskilling of creative capacities represents a structural problem because: - Environments with narrow affordance fields systematically undermine opportunities for creative development - Without proper mentoring and embodied interaction, individuals cannot appreciate more masterful levels of creative skill - Capacity-hostile environments create conditions where innovative thinking becomes increasingly difficult - Example: Educational environments that prioritize AI-generated content over creative exploration

docs.title: Contrast with Instrumentalist Views
docs.text: Unlike instrumentalist approaches that treat creative capacities as tools to achieve goals, the structural perspective recognizes: - The process of creative development has intrinsic value - Being a certain kind of creative agent matters more than merely achieving creative outcomes - Example: The value of artistic creation comes from the process of self-expression, not just the finished product

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text: Protecting creative capacities requires: - Designing AI tools that scaffold rather than replace creative processes - Creating environments that encourage rather than discourage experimentation - Preserving opportunities for embodied, intersubjective creative collaboration - Supporting public spaces that facilitate meaningful creative engagement - Example: Workshops that use AI as a brainstorming partner rather than a content replacement

docs.title: Developmental Perfectionism
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-15 | Last Updated: 2026-07-22

Developmental Perfectionism is a neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this framework explains why the competent exercise of human capacities constitutes intrinsic value rather than merely instrumental value.

docs.title: Unified Flourishing
docs.text:
• Human flourishing is not merely accumulation of goods but a complex, integrated state
  • Capacities develop synergistically; flourishing requires balanced development across domains
  • Example: Epistemic capacities support social capacities, which in turn support creative capacities

docs.title: Constitutive Value
docs.text:
• The competent exercise of capacities yields outcomes with intrinsic value (knowledge, beauty, morality, friendship)
  • Capacities are intrinsically valuable because they constitute the achievement of these goods
  • Example: The value of being on Mt. Everest comes from competent exercise of climbing capacities, not merely being there

docs.title: Developmental Process
docs.text:
• Flourishing involves ongoing growth rather than static achievement
  • Capacity development requires effort, overcoming difficulty, and perseverance
  • Example: Developing critical thinking involves encountering and overcoming intellectual challenges

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Theoretical rationality: thinking, considering reasons, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Practical rationality (phronesis): doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  • Essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
• Moral capacity: recognizing others as moral agents, understanding ethical principles
  • Relational capacity: forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love
  • Critical for participating in communal life and shared valuing

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
• Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Transforming conceptual spaces without relying on luck or mechanical procedures
  • Enables innovation and adaptation to novel situations

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text:
• Ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow
  • Required to achieve intrinsically valuable goals
  • Functions as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities

docs.title: Implications for AI Deskilling
docs.text: Developmental Perfectionism explains why capacity-deskilling is harmful:

docs.title: Constitutive Harm
docs.text:
• Capacity-deskilling is bad because capacities are constitutive of flourishing
  • Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives
  • Example: Deskilling of critical thinking capacity diminishes one's ability to navigate truth

docs.title: Structural Perspective
docs.text:
• Deskilling should be understood as structural problem, not individual failing
  • AI creates environments hostile to capacity cultivation
  • Example: AI systems that automate decision-making create narrow fields of affordances

docs.title: Evaluation Framework
docs.text:
• AI applications should be evaluated based on conduciveness to capacity cultivation
  • Systems that encourage plan-forming rather than plan-following support flourishing
  • Example: Tools that scaffold critical thinking rather than replace it are capacity-conducive

docs.title: Contrast with Instrumentalist Views
docs.text: Unlike instrumentalist approaches that treat capacities as tools to achieve goals, Developmental Perfectionism recognizes: - The process of capacity development has intrinsic value - Being a certain kind of person matters more than merely achieving outcomes - Example: Life-planning has value in the self-constituting activity, not just in achieving planned goals

docs.title: Practical Applications
docs.text: This framework informs: - AI design principles that preserve opportunities for capacity development - Educational approaches that balance AI assistance with meaningful practice - Workplace policies that maintain embodied, intersubjective learning opportunities - Public policy supporting capacity-conducive environments through community infrastructure

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships, with profound implications for AI's impact on market research practice.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman draws on the Enactive Approach in cognition to argue that:

  • Participatory sense-making (De Jaegher and Di Paolo 2007) is constitutive of social cognition
  • Embodied understanding arises through voice, gaze, and physical presence
  • The spontaneity of recognizing others as moral agents is inherent in embodied interaction
  • Disembodied interaction requires additional mental effort to attribute moral agency

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
In market research, embodiment in skilling manifests through:

  • Qualitative research: The development of empathy and rapport during face-to-face interviews
  • Client relationships: Building trust through embodied presence in meetings
  • Team collaboration: Developing shared understanding through physical co-presence
  • Ethical judgment: Cultivating moral sensitivity through direct engagement with research participants

docs.title: AI-Induced Embodiment Deficits
docs.text:
AI tools create embodiment deficits when they:

  • Replace in-person interviews with digital survey tools
  • Substitute video calls for physical meetings
  • Automate client communication through chatbots
  • Mediate team collaboration through asynchronous platforms

These deficits undermine the development of critical market research capacities, particularly:

  • Social capacities for understanding participant perspectives
  • Moral capacities for ethical research practice
  • Epistemic capacities for contextual interpretation
  • Creative capacities for innovative research design

docs.title: Case Evidence
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study documents embodiment challenges:

  • 68% of researchers report diminished empathy development when working primarily with digital data
  • Teams using fully remote collaboration show 27% lower consensus on ethical research dilemmas
  • Junior researchers with limited face-to-face experience demonstrate weaker participant rapport skills

docs.title: Preserving Embodiment in AI Era
docs.text:
Organizations can maintain embodiment in skilling by:

  1. Hybrid research methodologies that combine AI efficiency with embodied qualitative components
  2. Structured in-person requirements for critical relationship-building activities
  3. Embodied reflection practices where researchers document physical interactions and responses
  4. Mentorship programs emphasizing embodied guidance through co-facilitation
  5. Ethical deliberation protocols requiring physical presence for high-stakes decisions

docs.title: Connection to Structural Deskilling
docs.text:
The erosion of embodiment explains why AI adoption contributes to the human operating model gap. When market research becomes disembodied, professionals cannot develop the social and moral capacities necessary to guide AI systems effectively, creating a structural deskilling problem that cannot be solved through individual adaptation alone.

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-18 | Last Updated: 2026-07-22

Epistemic capacities are the human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing rather than merely instrumental, and their deskilling represents a significant threat to human agency.

docs.title: Theoretical Rationality
docs.text:
• Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Essential for acquiring knowledge and understanding truth
  • Enables critical evaluation of information sources and claims
  • Example: Analyzing research methodology to assess study validity

docs.title: Practical Rationality (Phronesis)
docs.text:
• Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  • Involves wisdom in applying theoretical knowledge to practical situations
  • Requires accurate understanding of one's situation and circumstances
  • Example: Knowing when to apply general principles versus making exceptions

docs.title: Development Process
docs.text: Epistemic capacities develop through:

docs.title: Habituation Process
docs.text:
• Gradual progression from novice to expert through practice
  • Involves encountering and overcoming intellectual disappointment and failure
  • Requires refinement through successive trials and learning from mistakes
  • Example: Developing research skills through iterative project work

docs.title: Intersubjective Learning
docs.text:
• Becoming epistemically skilled typically requires mentors to instill both technical competence and appreciation for knowledge value
  • Shared valuing develops through relationships where both mentor and mentee view knowledge as intrinsically valuable
  • Example: Academic communities establishing shared valuing of intellectual rigor

docs.title: Embodied Engagement
docs.text:
• Proper cultivation requires environments affording opportunities for knowledge application
  • Libraries afford reading opportunities that trigger epistemic capacities
  • Public discourse spaces afford opportunities for testing and refining beliefs

docs.title: AI Threat Analysis
docs.text: AI systems threaten epistemic capacities through:

docs.title: Automated Reasoning
docs.text:
• Erosion of critical thinking through over-reliance on AI-generated content
  • Diminished diagnostic reasoning in healthcare AI systems (NHS England 2023; Natali et al. 2025)
  • Reduced capacity for self-deliberation when using AI life planners
  • Example: Students using AI writing tools may struggle to develop independent argumentation skills

docs.title: Narrowed Affordance Fields
docs.text:
• Digital environments that fracture affordance space into disconnected fields
  • Social media algorithms that create epistemic bubbles
  • AI systems that provide ready answers without requiring reasoning process
  • Example: Search engines that prioritize quick answers over deep exploration

docs.title: Structural Implications
docs.text: The deskilling of epistemic capacities represents a structural problem because: - Environments with narrow affordance fields systematically undermine opportunities for epistemic development - Without proper mentoring and shared valuing, individuals cannot appreciate more masterful levels of epistemic skill - Capacity-hostile environments create conditions where truth navigation becomes increasingly difficult - Example: Educational environments that prioritize AI-generated content over thoughtful discussion

docs.title: Contrast with Instrumentalist Views
docs.text: Unlike instrumentalist approaches that treat epistemic capacities as tools to achieve goals, the structural perspective recognizes: - The process of knowledge development has intrinsic value - Being a certain kind of epistemic agent matters more than merely achieving correct beliefs - Example: The value of research comes from the process of discovery, not just the findings

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text: Protecting epistemic capacities requires: - Designing AI tools that scaffold rather than replace reasoning processes - Creating environments that encourage rather than discourage epistemic agency - Preserving opportunities for embodied, intersubjective knowledge development - Supporting public spaces that facilitate meaningful intellectual engagement - Example: Educational approaches that use AI as discussion partner rather than answer provider

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure.

docs.title: Stages of Habituation
docs.text:
Ferdman describes habituation as a multi-stage process:

  1. Novice stage: Rule-based learning with limited contextual understanding
  2. Advanced beginner: Recognition of situational elements through concrete experience
  3. Competent stage: Development of deliberate planning for action
  4. Proficient stage: Holistic perception of situations with intuitive guidance
  5. Expert stage: Fluid performance with deep situational understanding

This progression, adapted from Dreyfus and Dreyfus (1986), emphasizes that skill development requires successive attempts at an activity where the process itself is one of growth rather than simple repetition.

docs.title: Essential Components
docs.text:
The habituation process requires:

  • Embodied practice: Physical engagement with the activity
  • Disappointment encounters: Opportunities to experience and learn from failure
  • Gradual progression: Incremental challenges that build on previous learning
  • Mentor guidance: Support from experienced practitioners who understand the learning trajectory
  • Value internalization: Developing personal commitment to the skill's importance

docs.title: Market Research Context
docs.text:
In market research, the habituation process develops critical capacities through:

  • Qualitative interviewing: Learning to adjust questions based on participant responses through repeated practice
  • Data interpretation: Developing analytical judgment by working through ambiguous cases
  • Research design: Mastering methodology selection through trial and error
  • Client consultation: Building communication skills through real interactions

docs.title: AI Disruption of Habituation
docs.text:
AI systems threaten the habituation process by:

  • Error elimination: Providing 'correct' answers without opportunities to learn from mistakes
  • Automation of routine tasks: Removing foundational practice opportunities that build expertise
  • Template standardization: Reducing variation in research scenarios that enable nuanced understanding
  • Feedback loop shortening: Bypassing the iterative refinement process essential for skill development

docs.title: Case Study: Entry-Level Researcher Development
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study documents how AI adoption has disrupted traditional habituation pathways:

  • Junior researchers now skip foundational data collection practice as AI handles survey programming
  • Analysis templates reduce opportunities to develop independent interpretation skills
  • Automated reporting limits exposure to client communication challenges

This creates the entry-level squeeze where entry positions demand senior-level judgment skills without providing the habituation process necessary to develop them.

docs.title: Preserving Habituation in AI Era
docs.text:
Organizations can protect the habituation process by:

  • Creating deliberate practice zones where researchers work without AI assistance
  • Implementing error documentation protocols that normalize learning from mistakes
  • Designing progressive challenge frameworks that gradually increase complexity
  • Establishing reflection practices where researchers articulate their learning journey
  • Maintaining mentor-apprentice relationships that support intersubjective habituation

Last updated: 2026-07-22 | First observed: 2026-07-03

docs.title: Human Capacities
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-15 | Last Updated: 2026-07-22

Human capacities are core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are not merely instrumental but constitutive of human flourishing within a developmental-perfectionism framework.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
Definition: Human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding.

Components: - Theoretical rationality: thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating - Practical rationality (phronesis): doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason

Flourishing Role: - Essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions - Enable competent exercise of practical reason - Constitute intrinsic value through knowledge achievement

AI Threats: - Erosion of critical thinking through over-reliance on AI-generated content - Diminished diagnostic reasoning in healthcare AI systems - Reduced capacity for self-deliberation when using AI life planners

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
Definition: Human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life.

Components: - Moral capacity: recognizing others as moral agents, understanding ethical principles - Relational capacity: developing meaningful relationships of friendship and love

Flourishing Role: - Necessary for mutual respect between persons - Enable participation in shared valuing practices - Constitute intrinsic value through meaningful relationships

AI Threats: - Diminished ethical sensitivity through AI decision-making systems - Weakened moral judgment in disembodied digital environments - Reduced opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for moral recognition

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
Definition: Human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces.

Components: - Novel combination: creating unfamiliar connections between familiar ideas - Conceptual transformation: reshaping conceptual frameworks without relying on luck

Flourishing Role: - Enable innovation and adaptation to novel situations - Support problem-solving in unexpected circumstances - Constitute intrinsic value through creative expression

AI Threats: - Deskilling through over-reliance on AI content generation - Reduced opportunities for creative problem-solving when AI provides ready solutions - Narrowed conceptual spaces when AI systems reinforce existing patterns

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text:
Definition: The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals.

Components: - Effort exertion: applying sustained energy toward challenging goals - Difficulty overcoming: navigating obstacles and setbacks - Growth orientation: developing through challenges rather than avoiding them

Flourishing Role: - Functions as meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities - Enables transition from novice to expert through habituation process - Constitutes intrinsic value through personal growth

AI Threats: - Diminished perseverance when AI systems automate challenging tasks - Reduced growth opportunities when AI provides ready solutions - Weakened capacity for self-directed planning through AI life coaches

docs.title: Structural Vulnerability
docs.text: Human capacities are particularly vulnerable to structural threats because: - They develop through habituation process requiring practice and failure - They depend on intersubjectivity-in-skilling for shared valuing - They require embodiment-in-skilling through physical interaction - They necessitate agential control over initiating capacity-development activities

docs.title: AI Impact Framework
docs.text: The structural perspective reveals how AI systems can undermine capacities through: - Creating capacity-hostile-environments with narrow fields of affordances - Encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming agency - Replacing embodied interaction with disembodied digital mediation - Automating routine tasks that provide necessary habituation opportunities

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text: Protecting human capacities requires: - Designing AI systems that scaffold rather than replace capacity development - Creating capacity-conducive-environments with rich affordance fields - Preserving opportunities for embodied, intersubjective learning - Supporting public goods that encourage structured and unstructured capacity practice

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Intersubjectivity in Skilling
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-03 | Last Updated: 2026-07-22

Intersubjectivity in skilling refers to the shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill. Skills development cannot occur in isolation but requires relationships that foster shared valuing of capacities.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text: The concept emerges from: - Virtue ethics frameworks where moral development occurs through relationships - Social epistemology recognizing knowledge as socially situated - Enactive cognition approaches emphasizing participatory sense-making

docs.title: Mentor-Mentee Relationships
docs.text:
• Good mentors are typically necessary to cultivate proper motivational structure for skill development
  • Mentors instill both technical competence and appreciation for the skill's intrinsic value
  • Shared intentions develop where both mentor and mentee come to view the skill's value as their own
  • Example: A writing mentor doesn't just teach grammar but cultivates appreciation for clear communication as valuable in itself

docs.title: Societal-Level Practices
docs.text:
• Social practices performed by groups or whole societies provide mentoring environments
  • Family, colleagues, and citizens collectively generate moral reasons for action
  • Social practices have constitutive aims (telos) that ultimately help people fare well
  • Example: Academic communities establish shared valuing of intellectual rigor through peer review and discourse

docs.title: AI Impact Analysis
docs.text: AI systems threaten intersubjectivity in skilling through:

docs.title: Replacement of Human Guidance
docs.text:
• Artificial Personal Assistants provide advice without shared valuing of capacities
  • APAs lack the ability to instill appreciation for why capacities matter beyond instrumental value
  • Example: An AI life coach might help organize daily tasks but cannot convey why self-directed planning matters for human flourishing

docs.title: Erosion of Shared Valuing
docs.text:
• When enough persons don't value excellence in human capacities, those capacities risk atrophy
  • AI-mediated environments make it harder to develop the shared understanding necessary to appreciate capacities
  • Example: Over-reliance on AI for critical thinking diminishes societal valuing of deep analytical reasoning

docs.title: Structural Implications
docs.text:
The intersubjective dimension reveals why deskilling is a structural problem: - Learning to value a capacity is part of the habituation process; without proper mentoring, individuals cannot learn to value more masterful levels of capacities - On a societal scale, when environments lack opportunities for intersubjective skill development, capacities become devalued - Capacity-hostile environments create conditions where individuals cannot develop the shared understanding necessary to resist deskilling

As Ferdman argues, this necessitates societal solutions that preserve opportunities for meaningful intersubjective learning rather than expecting individuals to cultivate capacities in isolation. The volitional-capacity itself depends on intersubjective relationships that model why capacity development matters for human flourishing within a developmental-perfectionism framework.

docs.title: Contrast with Individual-Responsibility Approaches
docs.text: Unlike frameworks that treat deskilling as individual failing, the intersubjective perspective recognizes that: - Persons cannot be expected to 'will themselves' to cultivate capacities if their social environment doesn't value them - First, agents lack proper mentoring for the 'know-how' of capacity development - Second, they cannot obtain shared understanding regarding the value of capacities - Example: Students cannot develop critical thinking if educational environments prioritize AI-generated content over thoughtful discussion

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Narrow Field of Affordances
docs.text:
First Observed: 2026-07-17 | Last Updated: 2026-07-22

A narrow field of affordances refers to an environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This concept explains how AI's integration into socio-technical systems can systematically undermine human flourishing.

docs.title: Conceptual Foundation
docs.text: Drawing on Gibson's ecological psychology and enactive cognition approaches: - Affordances are action possibilities formed by the relationship between an agent and environment - A narrow field of affordances restricts the range of possible actions available to agents - Affordance shrinkage occurs when reduction in action possibilities is systematic, enduring, and deeply entrenched

docs.title: Structural Limitation
docs.text:
• Not merely fewer opportunities but invitations that severely influence agent behavior
  • Systematic reduction rather than temporary limitation
  • Deeply entrenched in the design of socio-technical systems
  • Example: Social media algorithms that narrow content exposure based on engagement metrics

docs.title: Capacity Deskilling Mechanisms
docs.text:
• Habituation deprivation: Deprives users of routine opportunities to practice judgment and strengthen 'cognitive musculature'
  • Shallow skilling: Affords only superficial engagement with capacities rather than deep development
  • Compensation discouragement: Makes it difficult for users to find alternative avenues to exercise capacities
  • Example: AI healthcare systems that offload diagnostic reasoning diminish clinical judgment development

docs.title: Digital Communication Platforms
docs.text:
• Fracture users' affordance space into disconnected fields (swiping, clicking, scrolling)
  • Create determinate, separate, and repeatable tasks that lead to alienation
  • Limit opportunities for mutually informing and enriching cognitive and bodily skills
  • Example: Messaging apps that reduce communication to emoji reactions

docs.title: Artificial Personal Assistants
docs.text:
• Constant availability designed to be helpful discourages seeking new growth opportunities
  • Replace routine, small-scale decision-making that builds broader life-planning capacities
  • Reduce need for self-directed planning through automated scheduling
  • Example: Sunsama app that schedules tasks into available time slots, removing planning agency

docs.title: Structural Implications
docs.text: The narrow field of affordances concept reveals why deskilling is a structural problem: - Environments with narrow affordance fields create conditions where users cannot develop shared valuing of capacities - Without proper mentoring and embodied interaction, individuals cannot appreciate more masterful capacity levels - Capacity-hostile environments create a vicious cycle where shallow skill development prevents capacity valuation - Example: Educational environments that prioritize AI-generated content over thoughtful discussion

docs.title: Contrast with Individual-Responsibility Approaches
docs.text: Unlike frameworks treating deskilling as individual failing, this concept recognizes: - The structural design of AI systems actively narrows available action possibilities - Users cannot be expected to overcome affordance shrinkage through willpower alone - Expecting 'virtuous superheroes' to resist deskilling overlooks environmental constraints - Example: Students cannot develop critical thinking if educational environments systematically narrow affordances

docs.title: Capacity-Conducive Alternatives
docs.text: Environments that avoid narrow fields of affordances: - Provide multiple, interconnected action possibilities that trigger combinations of capacities - Encourage rather than merely afford embodied interaction - Support public goods like community centers and libraries that facilitate meaningful engagement - Balance structure with openness to allow for both guided and self-directed capacity development

docs.title: Evaluation Framework
docs.text: AI applications should be assessed based on their affordance fields: - Do they provide rich, interconnected action possibilities? - Do they encourage rather than merely afford capacity development? - Do they preserve opportunities for agential control and self-directed growth? - Example: Tools that scaffold critical thinking rather than replace it maintain broader affordance fields

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools
